title: The Taimanov Variation
subtitle: Delay every commitment until White shows a hand
summary: Black plays 2...e6 and 4...Nc6 without committing the d-pawn, the g-pawn, or even the kingside knight's square — keeping the option to transpose into Scheveningen, Kan, or Hedgehog structures depending on what White tries. This lesson explains why that flexibility is a weapon in its own right, and walks through the queenside expansion plan that makes the Taimanov a lasting favorite of positional players.

metadata.historicalContext: Named for Soviet grandmaster (and celebrated concert pianist) Mark Taimanov, who helped develop this flexible move order in the 1950s and 60s. Decades later the same e6-Sicilian complex produced one of the most celebrated games in world championship history: Karpov vs Kasparov, game 16 of their 1985 rematch, whose central knight maneuver earned the nickname 'the octopus knight.'

rootAnnotations.title: What this lesson teaches
rootAnnotations.body: The Open Sicilian lesson studied the c-for-d trade from the 2...Nc6 move order. The Taimanov reaches the same bargain through 2...e6 and 4...Nc6 instead — a small change with a large consequence: Black hasn't committed the kingside knight, the d-pawn, or the king's bishop yet, so the same position can become a Scheveningen, a Kan, or a Hedgehog depending on how White sets up. This lesson teaches that flexibility as a strategy in itself, plus the concrete plan every Taimanov game eventually reaches for: ...Qc7, ...a6, and ...b5 pushing for queenside space and counterplay.

annotations.body: Standard development, prepping the central trade the family study covered in depth.

annotations.title: The other side of the c-pawn
annotations.body: Where the Open Sicilian lesson developed ...Nc6 first, the Taimanov's defining choice comes here: a small, flexible pawn move that opens the dark bishop's diagonal and prepares ...d5 someday, without yet telling White anything about where the kingside knight or the d-pawn will go.
The same trade as always — a flank pawn for a center pawn, a half-open c-file banked for later.
This looks identical to the Open Sicilian's main move order, just with the moves reordered — e6 before Nc6 instead of after. Why does the order matter at all?

annotations.title: Delayed development, deliberately
annotations.body: It matters because Black still hasn't played ...d6 or ...Nf6, and won't commit either for several moves. That keeps the d-pawn's future square open (d6 versus staying on d7 for a while) and the kingside knight's route open (f6 versus e7). The immediate danger of this delay is real — see the variation on White's next move — but the payoff is a position that can meet several different White setups without having shown its own plan first.

annotations.title: The move-order trap
annotations.body: Developing the other knight instead looks equally natural, but it invites a concrete problem: White's centralized knight can jump into Black's position before the d-pawn is safely on d6.

annotations.title: The leap that punishes the delay
annotations.body: The knight heads for d6, where it would fork the king and disrupt Black's whole position with check. Black has no better answer than blocking the square immediately, a move later than the main line needed to.
A genuinely independent branch rather than a mistake: Black develops the kingside knight immediately and follows up with a pin instead of the queen move.

annotations.title: Pin Variation
annotations.body: Rather than the patient ...Qc7 setup, Black pins the c3-knight to the king at once, adding pressure to e4 a full move earlier than the main line manages. It's a sharper, more committal way to reach the same family of structures — real theory in its own right, recognized as the Taimanov's Pin Variation, though it gives up some of the flexibility that makes the main line so resilient.

annotations.title: Breaking the pin
annotations.body: White interposes a second piece on the same diagonal — once the knight is no longer the last thing standing between the bishop and the king, it can move freely again. A simple, standard answer to a pin with nothing forcing behind it.
The calm, most common response. White's other main try, the Maroczy Bind with an early c4, takes a completely different strategic approach — see the variation.

annotations.title: The Maroczy Bind approach
annotations.body: Instead of developing normally, White claims both central light squares with pawns before Black can strike at them with ...d5 or ...b5. This trades the sharp piece-play race of the main line for a long positional squeeze — Black answers with patient regrouping rather than immediate queenside expansion.
Even against the bind, Black keeps the same flexible development scheme — proof that the Taimanov's core idea travels across very different pawn structures.

annotations.title: The signature move
annotations.body: The queen develops to an active square that avoids blocking any pawn or piece, eyes the long b8-h2 diagonal for a future battery with a rook or bishop, and still commits to nothing about where the kingside knight or the bishop will go. This one move is why the Taimanov has a reputation for flexibility beyond every other e6-Sicilian.

annotations.title: Clearing the path for ...b5
annotations.body: Takes b5 away from any White piece and prepares the queenside pawn storm that is the Taimanov's main source of counterplay — the same idea the Najdorf uses one tempo earlier, reached here by a different road.
Only now does the kingside knight commit to f6 — three moves later than in most other Sicilians, and on Black's own schedule rather than out of necessity.
Quiet development, keeping the king's path to safety clear.
The d-pawn finally commits, seven moves after e6 — supporting e5 for good and freeing the c8-bishop's development.

annotations.title: White's space grab
annotations.body: A common plan even with both kings already castled on the same side: f4 claims central and kingside space and prepares f5, pressing Black to react rather than simply build up.

annotations.title: Both plans, visible at once
annotations.body: White's program: f4-f5 to gain space and attack, or Qe1-g3 and central maneuvering to press the d6/e5 complex. Black's program: ...b5 completing the queenside expansion prepared four moves ago, ...Bb7, and a rook to c8 down the half-open file — with the option to trade knights on d4 at any moment to relieve central pressure. Neither side has committed to a single plan; both are still choosing.

annotations.title: What you should have noticed
annotations.body: Three lessons: delaying commitment is itself a plan — keeping ...d6, ...Nf6, and ...Be7 unplayed for as long as possible let Black adapt to White's exact setup rather than guess at it in advance; that delay carries a real cost if abused, as the early ...Nf6 mistake showed; and the Taimanov's queenside counterplay (...Qc7, ...a6, ...b5) is the same engine that powers the whole Sicilian family, just reached with maximum flexibility. This structural family has produced real history — see Karpov vs Kasparov for a game built on exactly this kind of position.
